title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and progressive pulmonary fibrosis
subject: respiratory
summary: Diagnose IPF by multidisciplinary discussion from a UIP pattern on HRCT after excluding exposures, drugs and connective tissue disease; offer nintedanib 150 mg twice daily or pirfenidone titrated to 801 mg three times daily with liver test monitoring, plus oxygen, rehabilitation and early transplant or palliative referral.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Typical patient: over 60, often male and an ex-smoker, with months of progressive exertional breathlessness and dry cough, fine bibasal inspiratory ('velcro') crackles, and sometimes finger clubbing.

Exclude known causes: occupational and environmental exposures (asbestos, silica, birds, moulds), drugs (amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, methotrexate, bleomycin), connective tissue disease and fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

HRCT categories: UIP (subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing, with or without traction bronchiectasis), probable UIP (reticulation with traction bronchiectasis, no honeycombing), indeterminate for UIP, or alternative diagnosis.

Progressive pulmonary fibrosis (fibrotic ILD other than IPF): at least 2 of 3 within the past year with no other explanation: worse symptoms; absolute FVC fall of 5% predicted or more, or DLCO fall of 10% predicted or more; radiological progression.

Acute exacerbation: acute worsening of breathlessness, typically within 1 month, with new bilateral ground-glass opacity or consolidation on a UIP background, not fully explained by heart failure or fluid overload.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Thin-section HRCT chest (with prone and expiratory images) reported by a radiologist experienced in ILD.
Serology to look for connective tissue disease: ANA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, extractable nuclear antigens and myositis antibodies as indicated, and CK.
Full lung function (FVC, DLCO), 6-minute walk test with oximetry, and resting oxygen saturation or arterial blood gas.

Multidisciplinary discussion (pulmonologist, radiologist, pathologist) makes the diagnosis. If HRCT is not UIP, consider BAL and tissue sampling; transbronchial lung cryobiopsy is an acceptable alternative to surgical biopsy in experienced centres.
Screen for comorbidities: pulmonary hypertension (echo), lung cancer, obstructive sleep apnoea, reflux, coronary disease, anxiety and depression.

sections.title: Antifibrotic therapy
items: Offer an antifibrotic to patients with confirmed IPF: nintedanib or pirfenidone (conditional recommendations for both), chosen by comorbidity and side-effect profile. They slow FVC decline but do not reverse fibrosis; there is no FVC threshold for starting.

Nintedanib 150 mg twice daily with food, about 12 hours apart; reduce to 100 mg twice daily for diarrhoea or raised liver enzymes. It is also suggested for progressive pulmonary fibrosis (2022 conditional recommendation).

Pirfenidone with food: 267 mg three times daily for days 1 to 7, 534 mg three times daily for days 8 to 14, then 801 mg three times daily (2403 mg/day). Use high-factor sunscreen and avoid sun exposure.
Do not use prednisolone plus azathioprine plus N-acetylcysteine, warfarin without another indication, ambrisentan or imatinib to treat IPF.
Antacid drugs or antireflux surgery should not be used to improve respiratory outcomes in IPF (2022); treat symptomatic reflux on its own merits.
Nerandomilast 18 mg twice daily (oral PDE4B inhibitor, US approval 2025) is a newer option not covered by the 2022 guideline; specialist use where available.

sections.title: Supportive care
items: Long-term oxygen for significant resting hypoxaemia; ambulatory oxygen for exertional desaturation that limits activity.
Pulmonary rehabilitation; smoking cessation; influenza, pneumococcal and COVID-19 vaccination.
Refer eligible patients for lung transplant assessment early, at or soon after diagnosis rather than at end stage.
Advanced disease: early palliative care, advance care planning, and low-dose opioid for refractory breathlessness or cough.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Nintedanib: liver tests before starting, monthly for 3 months, then every 3 months. Interrupt or reduce for ALT or AST above 3 times the upper limit; avoid in moderate or severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B or C).

Pirfenidone: liver tests before starting, monthly for 6 months, then every 3 months; reduce or stop for ALT or AST above 3 times the upper limit. Avoid fluvoxamine (strong CYP1A2 inhibitor); smoking lowers drug levels.
Lung function (FVC, DLCO), symptoms, weight and oxygen needs every 3 to 6 months. A relative FVC fall of 10% or more, or DLCO fall of 15% or more, indicates significant progression.
Manage side effects early: loperamide and hydration for nintedanib diarrhoea; taking pirfenidone with meals for nausea; dose reduction before discontinuation.
Nintedanib increases bleeding risk: caution with full anticoagulation, recent bleeding or high cardiovascular risk; teratogenic, so use contraception.

sections.title: Acute exacerbation
items: Admit; look for and treat triggers and mimics: infection, PE, pneumothorax, heart failure and aspiration (CT pulmonary angiography, echo, cultures, viral PCR).
Oxygen (high-flow nasal oxygen if needed) to a safe saturation target; broad-spectrum antibiotics are commonly given until infection is excluded.
Systemic corticosteroids are suggested for most patients (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence; no standard dose).
Antifibrotic therapy is usually continued if tolerated.
In-hospital mortality is high: mechanical ventilation is usually not appropriate unless bridging to transplant. Discuss ceilings of care and involve palliative care early.

sections.title: Special situations
items: Other fibrotic ILD (RA-ILD, systemic sclerosis ILD, fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, unclassifiable ILD): treat the underlying disease; add nintedanib if it progresses despite standard management.
Surgery, bronchoscopy or lung biopsy can trigger an acute exacerbation; involve the ILD team before elective procedures.
Older or low-weight patients often need lower antifibrotic doses; reduce rather than stop.
India: exclude pulmonary TB (a common mimic and complication) before diagnosis and before any immunosuppression, and ask specifically about silica and bird exposure.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating IPF with corticosteroids or immunosuppression, which does not help and can cause harm.
Missing hypersensitivity pneumonitis or connective tissue disease, which need different treatment.
Stopping an antifibrotic for manageable GI effects instead of dose reduction and symptom control.
Late referral for transplant assessment or palliative care.

drugs.name: Nintedanib
drugs.dose: 150 mg orally twice daily with food, about 12 hours apart
drugs.notes: Reduce to 100 mg twice daily for intolerance or raised liver enzymes. Avoid in moderate or severe hepatic impairment; bleeding risk; teratogenic.

drugs.name: Pirfenidone
drugs.dose: 267 mg orally three times daily for 7 days, then 534 mg three times daily for 7 days, then 801 mg three times daily (2403 mg/day), with food
drugs.notes: Photosensitivity, rash, nausea. Avoid with fluvoxamine, in severe hepatic impairment and with CrCl below 30 mL/min.

drugs.name: Nerandomilast
drugs.notes: PDE4B inhibitor approved in the US in 2025; not in the 2022 guideline. Diarrhoea is common. Specialist use.

drugs.name: Loperamide
drugs.dose: 4 mg orally at the first loose stool, then 2 mg after each loose stool (max 16 mg/day)
drugs.notes: Nintedanib-associated diarrhoea; start at first sign, with fluids.
